title: Shesha's hoods over the river
hookLine: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into the rain carrying a newborn
carry: seva: serving the Lord in every form
tomorrow: who is waiting on the other side of the river?

cards: The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. Prompted by the Lord himself, the Bhagavata says, Vasudeva picks up his son, and the prison starts to come undone.
The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low.
Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river.

teach.b: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, at night, in the rain.
The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests follows behind Vasudeva and spreads his hoods over father and child like an umbrella. Think about who Shesha is. In the ocean of milk, he is the Lord's bed.
On this road, he's the Lord's umbrella.

And the seventh child, drawn from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, Balarama, is a part of Shesha too, born to be the Lord's older brother; in many tellings of the Ramayana he came before as Lakshmana, Rama's brother.
Bed, umbrella, brother: devotees read it this way, whatever the Lord needs, Shesha becomes.
Hindus call that seva, service offered to God, and count it as worship in itself. It's why devotees are glad to sweep the temple floor, cook for a festival, or carry the deity in a procession.
Then the river. The Yamuna is swollen and fast, full of waves and whirlpools, and it makes way, the text says, as the ocean once gave way for Rama on his road to Lanka.

Later retellings add a basket on Vasudeva's head and the river rising to touch the child's feet; the Bhagavata's own account is shorter. A father, a child, a river giving way, and a serpent holding off the rain.

how: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and Vasudeva carrying the infant under Shesha's hoods is a familiar image in Hindu art. Seva, service offered to God, is lived in temple and festival work: cleaning, cooking, serving food and carrying the deity in procession.

o: the great serpent Vishnu rests on, sheltering the child
the river goddess who parts the Yamuna's flood
the serpent who guards the doors of Kamsa's jail

p: spreads his hoods against the rain
gives way, as the ocean did for Rama
a part of Shesha, born as the Lord's brother

s: in the Bhagavata, the river rises to touch the baby's feet
that comes from later retellings; the Bhagavata simply says the river gave way.
Shesha shelters the father and child from the rain
the serpent follows and spreads his hoods over them.
Shesha is only the serpent Vishnu lies on
tonight he's the Lord's umbrella, and he is born as Balarama, the Lord's brother.

games.q: you're Vasudeva. the doors are open, it's pouring, and the river ahead is in flood. what do you do?
o: wait in the prison for the storm to pass.
walk out into the storm with the baby.
hide the baby somewhere in the city.
games.why: he walks out at once, carrying his son himself, while Shesha shelters them and the Yamuna makes way.

practice: Do one small piece of seva today, offered rather than noticed: wipe the shelf where your family prays, wash the pots after someone cooks, or set out fresh water or a flower.
If you pray, offer it as you do it, the way Shesha holds his hoods over the Lord. If you don't, do it quietly for someone who won't find out it was you.

wordCard.voice: Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who spreads his hoods over Vasudeva and the newborn child in the storm.

orig.note: shesha: the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who shelters the child in the storm.

carryVoice: Seva: serving the Lord in every form, the way Shesha does. That's the week: prasad, the divine even in a dog, heaven that isn't the end, God coming down, then remembering him, loving him as a child, and serving. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.3.47–50: Vasudeva takes the child, the guards sleep, the doors open, Shesha shelters them, the Yamuna gives way as the ocean did for Rama
Bhagavata Purana 10.1.24 and 10.2.8 (Ananta, Shesha, to be born first as the Lord's elder brother; the child moved to Rohini is a part of Shesha)
